title: Pilgrims' roads
hookLine: Canterbury, Santiago, Rome: people walked a long way to reach a holy place

lines: A SCALLOP SHELL ON A STICK.
cards: Why would anyone leave home on foot to reach a grave? Part of the answer hangs from a walking stick: a scallop shell, tied on with a bit of cord. That's how you'd know someone was on the road to Santiago.

Blisters, a small bag, a hat against the sun. They left home long ago, and won't sleep in their own bed for a long time yet. In Chaucer's tales, a company on horseback trades stories on the way to Canterbury.
On another road, travelers climb toward Rome. Different roads, one question underneath.

teach.h: A GRAVE OR A SHRINE AT THE END.
teach.b: Each road ended at a grave or a shrine. Rome, where tradition says Peter and Paul are buried.
Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, where tradition places the tomb of James the apostle, and where the scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge.
Canterbury, in England, where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in his own cathedral and then honored as a saint.

People went to ask for healing, to give thanks, to do penance for a wrong, to keep a promise. Some, honestly, for the adventure: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is full of pilgrims who talk more than they pray.
But the road itself mattered. Leaving home meant leaving your comfort, your title, your routine.
On the road, a merchant and a farmer could sleep in the same hostel and eat the same soup, and monasteries and towns along the way took pilgrims in.

teach.h: STRANGERS AND PILGRIMS ON THE EARTH.
teach.b: Hebrews says the faithful of old confessed, in the King James Bible, "that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." A Psalm that longs for God's house blesses the one "in whose heart are the ways of them."

And tradition says pilgrims sang another Psalm as they climbed toward Jerusalem: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Christians haven't all agreed about pilgrimage.
Some reformers later criticized it, saying God is just as near at home. Catholic and Orthodox Christians still go, and so do others, on foot.
And some walkers say the same surprising thing: the road became the prayer.

how: Christians, and others too, still walk the Camino to Santiago de Compostela, carrying a scallop shell and collecting stamps in a pilgrim passport, and pilgrims still travel to Rome, Canterbury, the Holy Land and other shrines.

games.q: you're a medieval merchant who has reached a pilgrim hostel at dusk. a muddy farmer is sitting at the only free place at the table. what do you do?
o: demand a better room for a man of your standing.
sit down beside him and share the soup.
games.why: on the road, titles counted for less. a merchant and a farmer could sleep in the same hostel and eat the same soup.

practice: Think of a place within walking distance that means something to you: a church, a park, a grave, a tree, a friend's front door.

Picture setting out without your phone in your hand, carrying one intention, thanks, a worry or a person. If you pray, pray along the way in your mind; if you don't, let each pictured step be the attention.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrims' roads. The roads to holy places like Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, walked for healing, thanks or penance, where the journey itself becomes part of the prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the road is the prayer. Every road began at someone's front door. Day eight hundred forty-two, complete.
